title: D is for DE-ICING: How to survive the quiet killer in winter weather | MSFS A-Z
description:
Picture this: You're cruising comfortably, wrapped in thick clouds. Everything seems completely fine, but silently, your aircraft is getting heavier. Suddenly, your airspeed indicator starts acting completely erratic, the cockpit fills with alarms, and you realize your wings are choked in ice. In flight simulation, ice is the quiet killer—and it strikes when you least expect it.

Welcome back to Microsoft Flight Simulator A to Z! In this episode, we are conquering the cold with the letter D for De-icing. A lot of simmers treat ice as a purely cosmetic feature that just looks cool on the windshield. But Microsoft Flight Simulator actually simulates structural weight, aerodynamic drag, and critical instrument failures. If you want to fly safely through winter weather, this video is your ultimate guide. We break down the exact physics of the freeze, explain the critical difference between anti-ice and de-ice systems, and jump directly into the cockpit of the TBM 930 to demonstrate a worst-case scenario and how to recover before you stall.

In this video, you’ll discover:

The Icing Hazards: The core differences between Rime Ice, Clear Ice, and the deadly dangers of Pitot Icing.

The Pitot Tube Illusion: Why a frozen sensor will cause your airspeed indicator to falsely show you are speeding up during a climb.

Prevention vs. Removal: How hot bleed air (Anti-Ice) differs fundamentally from pneumatic de-ice boots (De-Ice).

Debunking the Bridging Myth: Why waiting for ice build-up is dangerous and why you should pop your airframe switches immediately.

Live In-Cloud Recovery Demo: Step-by-step cockpit management in the TBM 930 to clear your wings, restore your instruments, and break out safely into clear skies.

🕒 Chapters
00:00 - Intro
01:17 - Hazard theory
02:33 - Prevention vs. removal
03:46 - Demo

Mastering your ice protection systems transforms winter flying from an unpredictable guessing game into a highly rewarding, realistic piloting experience. Before your next cold-weather flight, make sure to add structural and probe icing checks to your climb and descent checklists.
